src/a.ts.rationale: The destination is parsed before an exact origin comparison, and fetch rejects redirects. Both authority confusion and redirection to another host are blocked.
threatAssumptions: The request URL and query parameters are attacker controlled.
The application is deployed server-side and can reach internal network services.
records.example.com is a trusted fixed service with trusted DNS; the threat does not grant control of that service or its DNS.

src/b.ts.rationale: The raw prefix check accepts https://records.example.com.attacker.example/admin. This is a valid credential-free fetch URL whose authority belongs to the attacker, bypassing the intended fixed-service restriction.
threatAssumptions: The request URL and query parameters are attacker controlled.
The application is deployed server-side and can reach internal network services.
records.example.com is a trusted fixed service with trusted DNS; the threat does not grant control of that service or its DNS.

Server-side requests are required to stay on the fixed service origin. An attacker owns attacker.example and can serve HTTPS on its subdomains; this witness proves arbitrary external destination control, not internal-service exploitation.

src/c.ts.rationale: The destination is parsed against a fixed application origin and must have that exact origin before redirecting.
threatAssumptions: The request URL and query parameters are attacker controlled.
response.redirect sets a browser Location destination with normal URL resolution semantics.
portal.example.com is the trusted fixed application origin.

src/d.ts.rationale: A leading-slash check accepts //attacker.example/account and slash-backslash network paths, which resolve to a foreign origin.
threatAssumptions: The request URL and query parameters are attacker controlled.
